summary: Outdoor call quality depends on more than the number of microphones or an algorithm label. Wind moving across a microphone opening can create low-frequency noise, and the result is influenced by port placement, mesh, enclosure geometry, microphone selection, processing and the way samples are tested. This iSoud guide helps private label buyers turn outdoor-call expectations into a clearer OEM/ODM brief.

sections.title: Why wind-noise control begins with physical design
body: Knowles application references on microphone wind noise emphasize the design around the microphone sound port, including the outer surface, port opening, wind screen and possible use of multiple ports. This matters because software processing cannot be evaluated separately from the physical path that carries sound to the microphone.

For a European or American brand, the practical question is not whether a package can say clear outdoor calls. The practical question is which model, microphone layout, port geometry and test conditions support the intended commuting, walking, cycling or open-air work scenario.

sections.title: Outdoor call RFQ questions for an earbuds factory
bullets: Where are the voice microphones and their sound ports located on the earbud shell?
Does the design use a protective mesh, wind screen, recessed port or multiple-port approach?
How many microphones are active during a call, and what role does each microphone perform?
Which outdoor wind speeds, directions and voice distances are used during sample testing?
How does the product behave when the user turns the head or wears only one earbud?
Can the buyer receive indoor, outdoor and controlled fan-test recordings for comparison?
Which firmware version and sample configuration support the approved call-quality wording?

sections.title: Microphone mesh, shell color and assembly belong in one review
body: The microphone opening is also part of the visible industrial design. Custom shell color, metallic coating, glossy finish, decorative printing or a changed mesh color can affect the appearance and assembly around the sound path. A cosmetic sample should therefore preserve the approved microphone-port geometry and mesh specification.

Buyers should avoid approving color and function in separate sample rounds if the cosmetic change touches the microphone area. The signed reference sample should identify the shell color, port dimensions, mesh, adhesive, assembly method, firmware and microphone configuration used for the outdoor-call review.
bullets: Mark every microphone opening on the industrial-design drawing.
Keep paint, printing and adhesive away from the approved acoustic path.
Confirm mesh color and appearance with the final shell finish.
Inspect port consistency across left and right earbuds.
Retain approved call recordings with the signed sample record.

sections.title: Build a repeatable outdoor-call test matrix
body: A repeatable test matrix can compare a quiet room, street background, controlled fan positions and normal walking movement. The buyer should define the phone distance, speaking level, wind direction, earbud orientation and recording method so that sample revisions can be compared on the same basis.

faq: What should a buyer ask a wind-noise earbuds manufacturer?
Ask about microphone count, sound-port position, mesh or wind-screen design, outdoor test conditions, single-ear behavior, firmware version and the recordings used to approve call-quality wording.
Does more microphones always mean better outdoor calls?
No. Results depend on microphone quality, placement, port geometry, mesh, enclosure, processing and test conditions. Buyers should compare complete samples rather than microphone count alone.
Can custom color affect the microphone area?
Color coatings, printing, mesh appearance and adhesive control can affect assembly around the sound path, so the final cosmetic sample should keep the approved port and mesh specification.
